summary: Describes an LDAP extended operation that reverses the roles of client and server for the rest of a session, or lets each peer act as both. It is experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4531 defines an LDAP operation that swaps the jobs of the two ends of a connection. After it, the side that was the client acts as the server, or, if both sides agree, each can act as either. The point is to let a directory server ask another one for something without having to invent a whole new kind of connection.

what is the ldap turn operation
how do i reverse client and server roles in ldap
subtitle: An LDAP extension that lets a connection flip, so the original client becomes the server, or lets both sides act as both.

tldr.problem: LDAP sessions are normally started by the client, so a server that wants to make the request has to build a whole new kind of session, with new authentication and security mechanisms to go with it.
tldr.mechanism: The memo adds a Turn operation, an LDAP extended operation with the object identifier 1.3.6.1.1.19, that asks the peer to swap roles. The request carries a flag for whether both peers may act as client and server, and each peer then authenticates again in its new role.
tldr.outcome: The document gives three authentication scenarios, covering TLS with simple authentication, TLS with SASL EXTERNAL, and mutual authentication with SASL EXTERNAL, and asks that the operation be restricted to authorized clients. It is an Experimental specification.

today: RFC 4531 is an Experimental document published in June 2006. It was later updated by RFC 8996, which deprecates TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 and updates the documents that refer to them.

sections.title: Why an Operation That Reverses the Roles
sections.content:
LDAP is a client-server protocol that typically operates over reliable octet-stream transports, such as TCP, and generally the client initiates the stream by connecting to the server's listener at some well-known address. There are cases where it is desirable for the server to initiate the stream. Although it is certainly possible to write a technical specification detailing how to implement server-initiated LDAP sessions, that would require the design of new authentication and other security mechanisms to support server-initiated sessions.

Instead, the memo introduces an operation, the Turn operation, which may be used to reverse the client-server roles of the protocol peers. This allows the initiating peer to become the server after the reversal. As an additional feature, the Turn operation may be used to allow both peers to act in both roles, which is useful where both peers are directory servers that desire to request, as LDAP clients, that operations be performed by the other. That may be useful in replicated or distributed environments.

The operation is intended to be used between protocol peers that have established a mutual agreement, by means outside of the protocol, that requires reversal of the client-server roles, or allows both peers to act both as client and server.
sections.plainLanguage: Normally the client calls and the server answers. Sometimes you want the other way round, so the two ends swap jobs. The memo adds an operation that does the swap, so that no new authentication machinery has to be invented.

sections.title: The Turn Request and Response
sections.content:
The Turn operation is defined as an LDAP Extended Operation identified by the 1.3.6.1.1.19 OID. Its function is to request that the client-server roles be reversed, or, optionally, to request that both protocol peers be able to act both as client and server in respect to the other.

The Turn request is an ExtendedRequest where the requestName field contains the 1.3.6.1.1.19 OID and the requestValue field is a BER-encoded turnValue, which holds a mutual flag and an identifier. A TRUE mutual value asks to allow both peers to act both as client and server, and a FALSE value asks to reverse the client and server roles. The value of the identifier field is a locally defined policy identifier, typically associated with the mutual agreement for which the turn is being executed.

The Turn response is an ExtendedResponse in which the responseName and responseValue fields are absent. A resultCode of success is returned if and only if the responder is willing and able to turn the session as requested; otherwise a different resultCode is returned.
sections.plainLanguage: The request carries a yes-or-no flag for whether both sides may act as client and server, and a text identifier for whatever agreement the two sides made. The answer is simply success or another result code.

sections.title: Authentication After the Turn
sections.content:
The extension's authentication model assumes separate authentication of the peers in each of their roles, and a separate Bind exchange is expected between the peers in their new roles to establish identities in those roles. When the Turn completes, the responding peer in its new client role has an anonymous association at the initiating peer in its new server role. If the turn was mutual, the authentication association of the initiating peer in its pre-existing client role is left intact at the responding peer in its pre-existing server role; if the turn was not mutual, that association is void.

The memo then shows three scenarios. With TLS and simple authentication, TLS is started and the initiating peer establishes its identity with the responding peer before the Turn, using the distinguished name and password mechanism of the Simple method of the Bind operation; after the turn, the responding peer in its new client role establishes its identity with the initiating peer in its new server role. With TLS and SASL EXTERNAL, each peer provides a valid certificate and the identity is established through the EXTERNAL mechanism of the SASL method of Bind, before and after the turn in the same way. With mutual authentication and SASL EXTERNAL, a GSSAPI mutual-authentication exchange is completed before the turn, and after the turn the responding peer in its new client role asks the initiating peer to use an external identity to establish its LDAP authorization identity.

The layers are unchanged by the extension: the LDAP message layer sits on the SASL layer, which sits on the TLS layer, which sits on the transport connection. The general restrictions against multiple TLS layers and against multiple SASL layers remain, and although the client and server roles in LDAP, and hence in SASL, may be reversed in subsequent exchanges, only one SASL security layer may be installed at any time.
sections.plainLanguage: Swapping roles does not carry the old credentials over. Each side proves who it is again in its new job, and the order of checks matters: the encryption comes first, then the turn, then the second side identifies itself.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The memo warns implementors that reversing the client and server roles, or allowing both peers to act as client and server, likely introduces security considerations not foreseen by its authors, and that the security implications of the design choices made in the authentication and data security models are not fully studied. It hopes that experimentation with the extension will lead to a better understanding of these models and to appropriate considerations being documented in a future document.

The considerations that are apparent at the time are these. Implementors should take special care to process LDAP, SASL, TLS and other events in the appropriate roles for the peers, because although the Turn reverses the client and server roles with LDAP, and in SASL authentication exchanges, it does not reverse the roles within the TLS layer or the transport connection. The responding server, the original server, should restrict use of this operation to authorized clients, and a client's knowledge of a valid identifier should not be the sole factor in determining whether it is authorized to turn. Where the peers expect to establish TLS, TLS should be started prior to the Turn and any request to authenticate via the Bind operation. The LDAP security considerations generally apply to the extension.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo is open about the risk: reversing roles changes who is allowed to ask for what, and the authors do not claim to have fully worked out the consequences. It asks servers to allow the turn only to clients they have authorized, rather than to anyone who knows a valid identifier.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: IANA has registered an LDAP Object Identifier to identify the LDAP Turn Operation, and has registered the LDAP Protocol Mechanism described in the document, with the object identifier 1.3.6.1.1.19, the description LDAP Turn Operation, and the usage Extended Operation. The values follow the requirements listed in RFC 4520.
sections.plainLanguage: The operation has its own number, 1.3.6.1.1.19, registered so that clients and servers can agree on what the request means.

data.code:
Turn request: ExtendedRequest
  requestName:  1.3.6.1.1.19
  requestValue: BER-encoded turnValue

turnValue ::= SEQUENCE {
     mutual         BOOLEAN DEFAULT FALSE,
     identifier     LDAPString
}

viz.caption: THE EXCHANGE WITH TLS AND SASL EXTERNAL

messages.label: BIND (SASL EXTERNAL) REQUEST
messages.note: A establishes its identity as the client.

messages.label: TURN (TRUE, XXYYZ) REQUEST
messages.note: The roles are reversed: A becomes the server.

messages.label: BIND (SASL EXTERNAL) REQUEST
messages.note: B, now in its client role, establishes its identity.
